name: Iris Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions or government. Your answers are confidential. What does an ordinary shift look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the excavator crew at Copper Plain mine and drive the machine when the rock face is awkward. My two-year technical diploma taught me the machine, and years watching loose edges taught me caution. My partner and I have grown children and more than six months of expenses saved. I have never used an AI tool; I keep a paper fault book beside the cab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that if AI only shortens office forms, our work at the face stays the same. I would keep the paper fault book and inspect the bucket teeth. A smooth form does not hold loose rock in place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wage is good and there are several other mines nearby. We have enough saved to wait out a short break in work. I would feel secure, though I would still check the pension statement before naming a retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep running the excavator and checking the edge before each load. I would ask payroll for a pension statement this year and compare it with household bills. I would let the office handle its own new forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I know the machine, and the household can manage ordinary surprises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you write in the fault book?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bucket tooth number, the hour and where I heard a knock. A mechanic can follow that without guessing. The fault book has earned its place in my cab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try an AI fault app?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the mine required it and someone showed me plainly. I do not use one now. A paper book works because the next shift can see what I saw.

I would keep the **paper fault book** in my cab.
think: My **wage and savings** make a short work break manageable.
I want **pension figures** before setting a retirement date.

**Request** a pension statement and compare it with household bills.
feel: **Calm** about work and ordinary household costs.

fieldNote: She is a **skilled crew lead** who trusts physical inspection and a paper log.
Higher pay, **strong savings** and nearby mines support calm in the mild picture.

steps.text: Keep operating Copper Plain excavator and inspecting face
Request pension statement before naming retirement date

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say planning and buying software might change the office, but the excavator still needs a driver. I would ask the foreman to keep the apprentice on the face with me. A young operator learns a loose edge by seeing one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own pay looks safe while robots spread slowly. I would worry if a new plan cut time for training or asked us to take more loads without checking the wall. The office might shrink, but I cannot judge its jobs from the cab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the new loading plan on paper and mark the unsafe edges. I would keep the apprentice beside me for the first month and record any load target we could not meet safely. If the foreman removed that training time, I would ask him to restore it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the crew and the new targets, not frightened for my own wage yet. I do not like paper targets that pretend rock is even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show the apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hairline crack above the bucket at the north face. I would make the apprentice stand back and see what falls when the machine moves. A training screen cannot teach the sound of rock cracking above an excavator bucket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you argue against all new planning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, a better delivery plan could save time. I would judge it by the wall and our actual loading hours. I just will not sign an unsafe target to please a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that full thinking AI by 2028 changes plans first, while capable robot excavators appear around 2031. Copper Plain might buy them. I would ask the mine for a written equipment schedule and proper paid apprenticeships before jobs changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty when thinking AI arrives and sixty-three when capable robots follow. If the mine bought robot excavators quickly, I might lose a high wage before our planned retirement. Our savings buy time, but I would not expect nearby mines to stay the same forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would delay the plan to buy a new caravan and ask for pension figures at sixty-three and sixty-five. I would keep driving after 2028 while the mine still needs operators. If Copper Plain offered paid mechanical instruction tied to a real repair post, I would take it without giving up my wage first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. We would not be ruined overnight, but I do not want to test retirement on a sudden layoff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children help if the wage stopped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They would bring groceries if needed, but my partner and I have saved so we can carry ourselves. I would rather find paid repair work. Our children have their own households.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why mechanical repair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know what a damaged bucket pin feels like from the cab. I would still need a fitter to teach the repair properly. A real apprenticeship beats a promise that a new screen will need a watcher.

I would request a **written equipment schedule** and paid training tied to posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years to thinking AI and about eight to capable robot excavators gives the mine time to teach new trades honestly. I would ask for an apprenticeship timetable with named places. The crew should know when equipment is ordered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty-three when planning changes in 2031 and about sixty-six when capable robots appear in 2034. If our pension figures work, I could retire before robot excavators replace drivers. If not, a paid repair post would be worth learning for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request pension projections for ages sixty-five and sixty-seven and compare them with our bills. I would keep mentoring the apprentice on the face. I would take a paid fitter course only if the mine posted a real repair job and kept my excavator wages during class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but able to make a measured choice. The extra years help if the mine tells the truth about jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge the fitter course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would speak to the maintenance lead and ask how many repair posts were actually funded. I would look at the equipment list, not a brochure. A fitter course with no paid repair job at the end would waste our time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if retirement is affordable at sixty-five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I might take it. I like the crew, but I do not need a second trade for pride. I would teach the apprentice properly before I left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a decade before thinking AI and about thirteen years before capable robot excavators is time for the mine to train young operators properly. I would ask for a clear equipment schedule. The family can make its own plans if it knows the facts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty-eight in 2036 and about seventy-one when capable robots arrive in 2039. I expect to be retired before then if the pension stays on course. Our savings and high wages make that possible, though I would keep checking the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep driving and teaching the apprentice while I still work. I would request an annual pension update and go through it with my partner. I would leave my paper fault book with the next crew lead when I retired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our own living, though I would worry for young operators with longer working lives. I want the mine to give them paid time to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a robot trial make you leave earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, a trial date is not my retirement plan. My partner and I would use the pension figure and our own wishes. I would not let a robot excavator set my family’s retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is in the fault book for the next lead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bucket teeth, cracked edges and the north face marks that trouble new drivers. I would walk the next lead through it in person. A paper book needs a living explanation too.

I would give young operators **paid learning time** while people still drive.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable robot excavators could arrive around 2031 before our planned retirement. A written equipment schedule and paid repair apprenticeship tied to a real post would help. I would want the pension figures first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who teaches a new driver to see loose rock above a bucket. I have stopped the excavator at Copper Plain mine for a hairline crack no printed plan showed. That judgement belongs in the next crew, whatever machine they use.

headlineQuote: I have stopped the excavator at Copper Plain mine for a hairline crack no printed plan showed.
portrait: Iris Santos is a **58-year-old** excavator crew lead at Copper Plain mine, with a technical diploma and grown children.
She earns **higher pay**, has substantial savings and can consider several nearby mines before retirement.
She has **never used AI**, relies on a paper fault book and teaches apprentices to spot loose rock.
Fast robot availability makes her **anxious** about wages; longer warning allows a funded retirement if pension figures hold.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because capable robot excavators could appear around 2031 before planned retirement.
whatWouldHelp: A **written equipment schedule**, paid repair apprenticeship linked to a real post and pension figures would help.
